(Right) Cayley graphs
Given a group G and subsets S ⊆G, the corresponding (right) Cayley graph, Cay(G, S), is the
labeled, directed graph on vertex set G with an edge labeled by s from g to h when h = gs for s ∈S.
Examples:
1. G = Z, S = {1}

2. G = Z, S = {2, 3}. Similar to above.
3. G = ⟨a, b : a2 = 1, b5 = 1, aba = b−1⟩, S = {a, b}. You can work it out for yourself, but we get two
“circles” acting in opposite directions, connected at each vertex bidirectionally by reflections.
4. G = F2 = ⟨a, b⟩, S = {a, b}. The Cayley graph is an infinite 4-regular tree, as each reduced word
represents a sequence of operations such that the inverse of a previous operation does not occur
after that operation.
5. G = ⟨a, b : aba−1b−1 = e⟩, S = {a, b}. The Cayley graph gives us good intuition that G ≃Z2.

Commutators (again!)
Recall, for g, h ∈G, their commutator is [g, h] = ghg−1h−1, and [g, h] = 1 ⇐⇒gh = hg by extreme
obviousness.
Further recall the commutator subgroup, or derived subgroup, G′ = [G, G], is ⟨[a, b] : a, b ∈G⟩.
More generally, for A, B ⊆G, define [A, B] = ⟨[a, b] : a ∈A, b ∈B⟩.
Lemma: Let G be a group, H ≤G. The following are equivalent:
(I) H ◁G
(II) [H, G] ≤H
Proof : Suppose H ◁G. Let h ∈H, g ∈G. [h, g] = h(h−1)g ∈H. So [H, G] ≤H.
Now suppose [H, G] ≤H. Let h ∈H, g ∈G. hg = h[h−1, g] ∈H. So H ◁G.
Certainly, we have [G′, G] ≤[G, G] = G′. So by the lemma, G′ ◁G.
Claim: For any group G, G/G′ is abelian.
Proof : Let aG′, bG′ ∈G/G′. (aG′)(bG′) = abG′ = [a, b]baG′ = ([a, b]G′)baG′ = bG′aG′.

sections.heading: As a universal property
sections.text: The abelianization of a group G is the quotient map q : G → G/G ′ . It is characterized by the following universal property : Given any abelian group A and any homomorphism ϕ : G → A , there exists a unique homomorphism ψ : G/G ′ → A such that ϕ = ψ ◦ q . Proof : Note that by the first IM theorem, G/ ker( ϕ ) ≃ im( ϕ ) ≤ A , so G/ ker( ϕ ) is abelian. Accordingly, G ′ ≤ ker( ϕ ). Thus, whenever gG ′ = hG ′ , we know that ϕ ( g ) = ϕ ( h ) since g − 1 h ∈ G ′ ≤ ker( ϕ ). We may thus unambiguously define ψ : G/G ′ → A by gG ′ �→ ϕ ( g ). Certainly, it works, so ψ is unique. 2
